parts:
Hi Eric/list,

I feel a bit responsible here, as I pointed Nicole to the Tweedie option
for her zero-inflated data (before she contacted the DS list). In fact,
in mgcv it is possible to fit the Tweedie distribution - the help is a
bit cryptic as it is not under 'family'; it is under 'Tweedie' (note:
see this within the mgcv, not the Tweedie, package, for a gam example -
copied below). It's not totally straightforward as it's not possible to
fit this distribution within the DSM engine - it can only (at present)
be done within R.

library(mgcv)
set.seed(3)
n<-400
## Simulate data (really Poisson with log-link)
dat <- gamSim(1,n=n,dist="poisson",scale=.2)
## Fit a `nearby' Tweedie...
b <- gam(y~s(x0)+s(x1)+s(x2)+s(x3),family=Tweedie(1.1,power(.1)),data=dat)
plot(b,pages=1)
print(b)
## Same by approximate REML...
b1 <-
gam(y~s(x0)+s(x1)+s(x2)+s(x3),family=Tweedie(1.1,power(.1)),data=dat,method="REML")
plot(b1,pages=1)
print(b1)
rm(dat)


Cheers,
Sharon.

Eric Rexstad wrote:
> > Nicole:
> >
> > I'm afraid it is not quite as simple as that. You'll note that the
> > line of code that you wish to change (the one that creates object
> > dsm.44) make a call to the function dsm.fit(). If you have a look at
> > that function, you will see that function in turn calls the function
> > gam() from the mgcv package (because the argument 'fn' requests the
> > fit of a gam).
> >
> > If you explore the R documentation for gam() in mgcv, you'll be
> > directed to the description of 'family' describing how you specify the
> > family of the error structure for your model. Tweedie is not one of
> > the choices available to you in the 'family' argument to gam().
> >
> > Instead you will need to investigate how to fit your model not using
> > the dsm.fit() function, but rather working from the constituent R
> > objects (sample.dat.44 and obs.dat.44) you will build the structure
> > necessary to fit your model with the error structure you desire. I've
> > not worked with fitting models with the Tweedie error structure, so I
